documentation.range: This species is distributed across the North Atlantic Ocean and into the adjacent Arctic Ocean. In the western Atlantic, it occurs from Disko Bay in southwestern Greenland (north to about 72°47'N), Davis Strait, Baffin Island (at about 72°N), Ungava Bay, Newfoundland and Labrador, the Gulf of St. Lawrence, and Nova Scotia in Canada to Virginia (37°50'N). In the eastern Atlantic, it occurs from southeastern Greenland (north to 69˚43'N), Iceland, the Barents Sea to Svalbard and Novaja Semlya (Russia), the Norwegian coast, Faroe Islands, Great Britain and Ireland to the North Sea, the western Baltic Sea south to the Bay of Biscay (Nielsen 1986, Haug 1990, Cargnelli et al. 1999, Mecklenburg et al. 2018). The depth range is 20-2,000 m (Klein-MacPhee 2002, Alfonso 2018, Mecklenburg et al. 2018, MFRI 2020).
documentation.population:
Eastern Atlantic: This species is naturally rare in Novaya Zemlya, the central and northern North Sea to the Skagerrak and Kattegat. It is common off Greenland, Iceland and in the southern Barents Sea (Mecklenburg et al. 2018). It is present in the western Barents Sea, which includes the continental slope region between mainland Norway and Svalbard, but is not common there; although, this may change as climate change progresses (M. Vihtakari pers. comm. 2021). ICES does not provide management advice for this species. The relative size of the Icelandic stock compared to the Norwegian stock is not known due to the limited availability of stock assessment data for the Norwegian stock. Research is currently underway to resolve this data gap. Norwegian commercial landings have been between 2,400 and 3,200 tons annually since 2015. Recreational landings in Norwegian waters are uncertain, but could be as high as 30% of commercial landings (Norwegian Institute of Marine Research pers. comm. 2021). Commercial landings in Icelandic waters averaged around 500-600 t annually from 1994 to 2010 before steeply declining due to a ban on directed fishing as well as mandatory release of live catches of this species, measures that have been in place since 2011 (MFRI 2020). 

In Norwegian waters, overfishing of this species began in the 1930s and catches and stock abundance declined steadily from the 1940s to the 1980s reaching a point of fishery collapse (Haug and Tjemsland 1986, Seitz et al. 2014). Most landings have been reported from central and northern Norway. By the early 2000s, north of 62°N, landings increased from 300-900 tons in the 1990s to 1,200-3,200 t from 2005 to 2019, and this is considered to indicate that some level of population increase has occurred in that area. However, landings south of 62°N remained low (50-100 tons) and there are no indications that the population in this area has increased since the period of collapse (1930 to 2005). Landings in Norway are now at the highest levels since the 1960s. Based on a survey conducted from 1995 to present, the species in Norwegian waters is at a time-series high; however, the trend is uncertain due to low selectivity of this species in trawl surveys. Currently, ~20% of commercial landings of this species is bycatch of other fisheries (Norwegian Institute of Marine Research unpublished data 2021). Increasing catches in the north may indicate an increase in abundance or increased fishing effort, and the low catch in the south may indicate a stock decline or reduced fishing effort (Høines et al. 2009). Landings by the Norwegian recreational fishery are substantial, but poorly documented (Ferter et al. 2017).   

In Iceland, the biomass and recruitment indices steeply declined from 1985 to 1990 and reached a historical low in 2008-2014. Surveys provided an index of total stock biomass for 1985-2020, but there was poor coverage of adult habitat. Stock indices steeply declined from 5,715 t in 1985 to 581 t in 1992 and remained low to 2020. The past five years have been somewhat higher than the period of historic low levels (2008-2014). Over the past 35 years, stock indices declined by 85%. Indices of spawning stock biomass (>66 cm) follow the same general pattern as total biomass. Recruitment has been declining over the past 20 years and since recruitment failure has occurred, the stock is expected to remain low into the near future despite low catches. It has been prohibited to target this species since 2012 and it is mandatory to release viable individuals when taken as bycatch. The reported number of releases has been increasing over the past 2-3 years (MFRI 2020).

Western Atlantic: This species was historically abundant from Nantucket Shoals to the Gulf of Maine, Gulf of St. Lawrence, Newfoundland Banks, the Labrador Shelf, and Flemish Cap (Cargnelli et al. 1999, Mecklenburg et al. 2018). The center of abundance in the northwestern Atlantic is generally considered to be located on the Scotian Shelf and Grand Banks (Beaty and Chen 2017).
 
In Canadian waters, this species is managed as two fishery stocks: the smaller one in the Gulf of St. Lawrence (Divs. 4RST) and the larger from the southern Grand Banks to the Scotian Shelf (Divs. 3NOPs4VWX5Zc). Longline surveys conducted on the Scotian Shelf and southern Grand Banks since 1998 are used to estimate an index of abundance for this species. Recruitment was relatively low in the 1980s and 1990s and spawning stock biomass declined by 77% from 1984 to 1993 and remained low for the subsequent 10-15 year period (NAFO 2009, NAFO 2011, Trzcinski et al. 2011, den Heyer et al. 2015). The reduction in fishing mortality since at least the late 1990s and six-year period of high recruitment from 2003 to 2009 have allowed the biomass to recover from historical overfishing. Abundance and landings have been increasing since the mid-2000s and the exploitation rate is currently at a historic low (Cox et al. 2016, Trzcinski and Bowen 2016). Scientific surveys conducted on the Scotian Shelf (Divs. 4VWX) since 1970, indicate increasing biomass at a relatively high rate since the early 2000s. The most recent biomass index in 2017 was the highest in the time series, but recruitment success may have been lower in recent years (DFO 2020). Survey indices on the Grand Banks have also been increasing since 2006 (den Heyer et al. 2015). The closure of several areas to fishing likely contributed to the increased productivity of this species (French et al. 2018). 

In the Gulf of St. Lawrence (Divs. 4RST), fisheries began targeting this species in the late 1800s. Landings steadily declined by 86% from over 650 t in the 1960s to 91 t in 1982 and began increasing again in the late 1990s. By 2019, catch was nearing 1,300 t, which is the highest catch level in the past 60 years. Catch per unit effort increased from an average of 100 kg per 1,000 hooks in the 2000s to 500 kg per 1,000 hooks in 2018 (DFO 2019). Survey indices of abundance also increased since 2005 (DFO 2019). Recruitment and abundance have been at historical highs as of 2017 and 2018. The exploitation rate trend is uncertain, but the total allowable catch limit has been reached every year since 2004. The survival rate of released bycatch varies by gear type with survival being high in longline fisheries but low in gillnet and demersal trawl fisheries. This introduces some uncertainty into the understanding of overall fishing mortality (DFO 2019). 

In U.S. waters, this species is managed as a single stock (Divs. 5YZ). It appears to be more abundant a short distance to the north in Canada despite equal availability of suitable habitat in the U.S. (French et al. 2018). This species was first targeted in U.S. waters by commercial fisheries in the 1800s in the Georges Bank-Gulf of Maine area and collapsed by the 1880s to early 1900s. The availability of historical data to reconstruct virgin biomass is limited, but the current stock size is likely at a small proportion of the virgin state. The most recent stock assessment was inconclusive due to limited availability of fishery-dependent and -independent data but pointed to the likelihood that the stock remains in an overfished state with some recent small increases. Survey indices of stock biomass and standardized fishery catch rates have been stable or slightly increasing since 2002 (Hansell et al. 2020). Uncertainty associated with stock structure and the possibility that the U.S. population has shifted northward as waters have warmed also contribute to the limited understanding of the stock status (Rago 2017). The exceptionally low catches of this species in the semi-annual trawl surveys conducted throughout the Gulf of Maine is thought to be due to both low abundance as well as its catchability in the survey gear (Beaty and Chen 2017). The continued lack of recovery in U.S. waters may be driven by historical overfishing, especially the repeated depletion of juveniles, and/or fine-scale stock structure characteristics (Seitz et al. 2016, Shackell et al. 2016, French et al. 2018). According to surveys conducted from 1965 to 2014, juvenile abundance was on average five times higher in Canada than in the U.S. Fishing mortality has been low in U.S. waters for several decades and it is unclear why biomass remains low as compared to the 1800s when it was abundant enough to support a large-scale fishery (Shackell et al. 2016). A tagging study conducted in the Gulf of Maine found evidence that mixing between the U.S. and Canadian stocks may occur and this has implications for the currently separate management regimes (Kersula and Seitz 2019).
documentation.habitats:
This large-sized, relatively cold-water, demersal species mostly occurs in habitats with water temperatures between 3 and 5°C and bottom depths of 10-300 m (Cargnelli et al. 1999, Alfonso 2018, Mecklenburg et al. 2018). Juveniles occur shallower than adults; adults seldom occur shallower than 60 m (Alfonso 2018). This species occurs on a variety of substrata, including sand, gravel, and clay bottoms, not on mud or rock bottoms (Scott and Scott 1988, Miller et al. 1991, Klein-MacPhee 2002, Alfonso 2018). It occasionally swims off the bottom into the water column for feeding (Alfonso 2018). It spawns in deep water on the outer continental shelf and upper slope from 200 to 700 m over soft bottom in European waters and over rough or rocky bottom in the western Atlantic (Cargnelli et al. 1999, Alfonso 2018, MFRI 2020). Spawning typically occurs from late winter to early spring in Canadian waters (Neilson et al. 1993); elsewhere, spawning occurs later (see details in Klein-MacPhee 2002). Adults occasionally undertake long distance migrations (Kersula and Seitz 2019). Seasonal migrations from deeper to shallower waters may be related to spawning (Le Bris et al. 2018) or feeding (Alfonso 2018). 

Diets are diverse and vary ontogenetically. Small fish (to about 30 cm) feed primarily on invertebrates (mostly annelid worms and crustaceans), then gradually adding fish to their diet as they grow. After about 80 cm, Atlantic Halibut feed almost exclusively on other fishes and squid (Bowman et al. 2000, Klein-MacPhee 2002, Alfonso 2018). Predators include seals, Greenland Shark, spiny dogfish, and goosefish (Bowman et al. 2000).

Growth rates vary depending on geographic area and sex (Alfonso 2018). For example, the growth rate is faster and maturity occurs earlier in individuals from more southerly parts of the range as compared to those inhabiting the northern part of the range (Shackell et al. 2019). Females exhibit faster growth than do males and also attain larger maximum sizes at least in the Gulf of St. Lawrence (McCracken 1958), and possibly elsewhere. The maximum length is 365 cm (Cargnelli et al. 1999, Mecklenburg et al. 2018, MFRI 2020).

Average age at maturity may occur around 5 years for males and 9 years for females, but maturity may occur as young as 4 years for males and 6 years for females off Labrador and Newfoundland (Bowering 1986). Length at first maturity is about 75-92 cm for males and about 103-155 cm for females (Sigourney et al. 2006, Armsworthy and Campana 2010, Trzcinski et al. 2011, Rago 2017, DFO 2019, MFRI 2020). Length at maturity declined in the western Atlantic as a result of heavy fishing (Coad et al. 1995, Mecklenburg et al. 2018). Longevity estimates may be underestimated, but it can reach at least 50 years of age (Muus and Dahlstrom 1974, Trumble et al. 1993, Armsworthy and Campana 2010, Karlson et al. 2013). Natural mortality is 0.1-0.15 (Brodziak 2002, Cox et al. 2016, Rago 2017). Generation length (1/adult mortality + age of first reproduction) is about 16-19 years.
documentation.threats: Historically, overfishing has been the major threat to this species. Its slow growth rate and late maturity causes it to be susceptible to rapid population declines when experiencing overexploitation (Sigourney et al. 2006, Høines et al. 2009). This species is also expected to be susceptible to negative impacts from warming water temperatures associated with climate change (Hare et al. 2016, French et al. 2018).
documentation.measures:
In Norwegian waters, the Skagerrak, and Sweden, fishing for this species is prohibited during the spawning season. In Swedish and Norwegian waters, trawlers have been outfitted with selection grids and escape panels to increase the survivorship of bycatch, including of this species. There is no maximum allowable catch limit in Norway, but the fisheries are regulated by minimum and maximum catch size limits, mesh size limits, gear restrictions, and seasonal area closures. Regulation and monitoring of the Norwegian commercial and recreational fishery needs improvement, including data collection (Høines et al. 2009, Ferter et al. 2017). The recent implementation of required reporting for the tourist recreational fishery has improved data availability. This species was assessed as Least Concern in the regional Red List assessment in 2015 by the Norwegian Biodiversity Information Center (Rødlisten = the Norwegian Red List) primarily based on improved recruitment in northern Norway, but this assessment needs updating given concerns for impacts from high fishing mortality (M. Vihtakari pers. comm. 2021). 

Stock assessment advice and fishery independent survey data for Icelandic waters are provided by the Marine and Freshwater Research Institute to advise regulations set by the Ministry of Industries and Innovation of Iceland. In Iceland, it is prohibited to target this species and it is mandatory to release viable bycatch. Research is needed on the adult abundance in Icelandic waters (MFRI 2020). This species was assessed as Vulnerable in the European regional Red List assessment conducted in 2014.

Regulation of this fishery in Canadian waters include total allowable catch limits, seasonal closures, vessel licensing, gear restrictions, bycatch limits and size limits. Fishery independent scientific surveys are conducted on the Scotian Shelf and southern Grand Banks and commercial catch is sampled to inform the stock assessment process that is conducted every two years (DFO 2019). The Canadian longline fishery has been certified sustainable by the Marine Stewardship Council since 2013. Studies on stock structure off Canada are needed especially as fishing effort is increasing and the sustainability of this fishery requires well-informed management (Shackell et al. 2019). 

In the U.S., trawl fisheries are not permitted to target this species, and each vessel can take only one individual as bycatch per trip. A longline fishery off Maine is permitted to target this species during a two-month season with restrictions on gear and total allowable catch (Hansell et al. 2020). Recreational fishers are permitted only one fish per trip with a size limit. Research is needed on the biological population structure of the U.S. and Canadian stocks to inform the need for collaborative management (French et al. 2018, Kersula and Seitz 2019). It has been listed as a 'species of concern' under the U.S. Endangered Species Act since 2004. Research is needed on the potential impact from changing water temperatures due to climate change and the consideration of expanding protections for juvenile habitat (French et al. 2018). Hare et al. (2016) concluded that this species is highly sensitive to climate change. Additional bilateral fisheries management efforts between the U.S. and Canada may help inform rebuilding in the U.S. fishery stock (Shackell et al. 2016).
documentation.use_trade: This is a commercially valuable species throughout its range. In Canada, Atlantic Halibut commands the highest price of all the flatfishes (Alfonso 2018). It is mainly taken in bottom longline, gillnet, and demersal trawl fisheries; in some areas, targeted fisheries for Atlantic Halibut still exist, while elsewhere, individuals can only be retained when taken as bycatch. It is also taken by recreational hook and line, which is partially catch and release.
documentation.rationale:
This widely distributed, cold-water, demersal species is large-bodied, relatively slow-growing, and long-lived. It is highly valued by commercial and recreational fisheries throughout its range and has experienced historical declines due to overfishing. It has an estimated generation length of 16-19 years. 

In Icelandic waters, total biomass and spawning stock biomass declined by 85% over the past 35 years (two generations). Despite the prohibition of directed fishing since 2012, the fishery stock is expected to remain well below historic levels in part due to recruitment failure. The fishery stock in Norwegian waters experienced a long period of collapse from 1930 to 2005 due to overfishing. Based on increases in commercial landings and a survey index, the fishery stock in Norwegian waters north of 62°N has been increasing since the early 2000s, but landings in the southern area remain low. In general, data are limited for the Norwegian fishery stock because the fisheries-independent surveys do not target this species and the recreational fishing catches are not well-documented. Research is currently ongoing to address these data gaps. Fishing for this species in Norwegian waters is subject to regulations, but negative impacts from exploitation remain a concern and efforts to improve fishery management are in development. 

The Canadian southern Grand Banks to the Scotian Shelf (Divs. 3NOPs, 4VW, X5Zc) stock is generally considered to be the center of abundance of this species in the western Atlantic. This stock declined sharply by 77% from 1984 to 1993 due to overfishing, but biomass has been increasing since the early 2000s, or over a little more than one generation, due to reduced fishing mortality and a period of high recruitment. The fisheries management and regulation that allowed the biomass to recover is expected to remain in place. Similarly, in the smaller Gulf of St. Lawrence stock (Divs. 4RST), abundance, recruitment, and landings have been increasing since the late 1990s and early 2000s and are currently at historic high levels. In U.S. waters (Divs. 5YZ), the stock status is relatively poorly understood due to the limited availability of key data. Survey indices of stock biomass and standardized fishery catch rates have been stable or slightly increasing since 2002, but biomass remains low compared to historical levels. Stringent management similar to that which Canada implemented are also in place in U.S. waters and the lack of recovery is not well-understood but could be caused by historical overfishing or a possible northward shift in the population as waters have become warmer. 

Intrinsic characteristics such as slow-growth and late maturity cause this species to be susceptible to rapid population declines under exploitation. There are varying types of restrictive fishing regulations in place through most of the distribution of this species. These conservation measures have allowed recovery from historical overfishing to begin, but it is highly likely that the population would rapidly decline if these fishing restrictions were removed. The population of this species has been increasing on a global level over the past generation but remains low compared to historical levels prior to severe overfishing. It is listed as Near Threatened based on its dependence on conservation measures currently in place, particularly as it is considered that the removal of any of the existing conservation measures would cause this species to rapidly decline. In addition to population monitoring and the continuance of fishing regulations, it is recommended to research potential impacts from climate change, biological population structure, and improve population data collection throughout the range of the species. 

The findings and conclusions in this document are those of the authors, and do not necessarily represent the views of the National Marine Fisheries Service.
